In [[geometry]], the '''triakis icosahedron''' is an [[Archimedean solid|Archimedean dual]] solid, or a [[Catalan solid]], with 60 [[isosceles triangle]] faces. Its dual is the [[truncated dodecahedron]]. It has also been called the '''kisicosahedron'''.<ref name=cbg>{{cite book|first1=John H.|last1=Conway|author1-link=John Horton Conway|first2=Heidi|last2=Burgiel|first3=Chaim|last3=Goodman-Strauss|author3-link=Chaim Goodman-Strauss|title=The Symmetries of Things|title-link=The Symmetries of Things|year=2008|publisher=AK Peters|isbn=978-1-56881-220-5|page=[https://books.google.com/books?id=Drj1CwAAQBAJ&pg=PA284 284]}}</ref> It was first depicted, in a non-convex form with [[equilateral triangle]] faces, by [[Leonardo da Vinci]] in [[Luca Pacioli]]'s ''[[Divina proportione]]'', where it was named the ''icosahedron elevatum''.<ref name=bpv>{{cite book
 | last1 = Brigaglia | first1 = Aldo
 | last2 = Palladino | first2 = Nicla
 | last3 = Vaccaro | first3 = Maria Alessandra
 | editor1-last = Emmer | editor1-first = Michele
 | editor2-last = Abate | editor2-first = Marco
 | contribution = Historical notes on star geometry in mathematics, art and nature
 | doi = 10.1007/978-3-319-93949-0_17
 | pages = 197–211
 | publisher = Springer International Publishing
 | title = Imagine Math 6: Between Culture and Mathematics
 | year = 2018| isbn = 978-3-319-93948-3
 }}</ref> The [[capsid]] of the [[Hepatitis A]] virus has the shape of a triakis icosahedron.<ref>{{cite journal
 | last1 = Zhu | first1 = Ling
 | last2 = Zhang | first2 = Xiaoxue
 | date = October 2014
 | doi = 10.1007/s13238-014-0103-7
 | issue = 2
 | journal = Protein & Cell
 | pages = 79–80
 | title = Hepatitis A virus exhibits a structure unique among picornaviruses
 | volume = 6| pmid = 25359464
 | pmc = 4312766
 }}</ref>

==As a Kleetope==
The triakis icosahedron can be formed by gluing triangular pyramids to each face of a [[regular icosahedron]]. Depending on the height of these pyramids relative to their base, the result can be either convex or non-convex. This construction, of gluing pyramids to each face, is an instance of a general construction called the [[Kleetope]]; the triakis icosahedron is the Kleetope of the icosahedron.<ref name=bpv/> This interpretation is also expressed in the name, [[Conway kis operator|triakis]], which is used for the Kleetopes of polyhedra with triangular faces.<ref name=cbg/>

{{multiple image|align=center|total_width=500
|image1=De divina proportione - Icosaedron Elevatum Solidum.jpg
|caption1=Non-convex triakis icosahedron drawn by [[Leonardo da Vinci]] in [[Luca Pacioli]]'s ''[[Divina proportione]]''
|image2=DU30 small triambic icosahedron.png|
|caption2=The visible parts of a [[small triambic icosahedron]] have the same shape as a non-convex triakis icosahedron
|image3=Triakis icosahedron kleetope of the icosahedron out 6.svg
|caption3=The [[great stellated dodecahedron]], with 12 pentagram faces, has a triakis icosahedron as its outer shell}}

When depicted in Leonardo's form, with equilateral triangle faces, it is an example of a non-convex [[deltahedron]], one of the few known deltahedra that are [[Isohedral figure|isohedral]] (meaning that all faces are symmetric to each other).<ref name=shep>{{cite journal
 | last = Shephard | first = G. C. | author-link = Geoffrey Colin Shephard
 | doi = 10.1023/A:1004838806529
 | issue = 1–3
 | journal = Periodica Mathematica Hungarica
 | pages = 83–106
 | title = Isohedral deltahedra
 | volume = 39
 | year = 1999}}</ref> In another of the non-convex forms of the triakis icosahedron, the three triangles adjacent to each pyramid are coplanar, and can be thought of as instead forming the visible parts of a convex hexagon, in a self-intersecting polyhedron with 20 hexagonal faces that has been called the [[small triambic icosahedron]].<ref>{{cite book
 | last = Grünbaum | first = Branko | author-link = Branko Grünbaum
 | contribution = Can every face of a polyhedron have many sides?
 | hdl = 1773/4593
 | isbn = 978-1-933223-17-9
 | pages = 9–26
 | location = Bedford, MA | publisher = Comap, Inc.
 | title = Geometry, games, graphs and education. The Joe Malkevitch Festschrift. Papers from Joe Fest 2008, York College–The City University of New York (CUNY), Jamaica, NY, USA, November 8, 2008
 | year = 2008
 | zbl = 1185.52009}}</ref> Alternatively, for the same form of the triakis icosahedron, the triples of coplanar isosceles triangles form the faces of the first [[stellation]] of the icosahedron.<ref>{{cite book
  | last = Cromwell
  | first = Peter R.
  | title = Polyhedra
  | publisher = Cambridge University Press
  | date = 1997
  | isbn = 0-521-66405-5
 | page = 270}}</ref> Yet another non-convex form, with [[Golden triangle (mathematics)|golden isosceles triangle]] faces, forms the outer shell of the [[great stellated dodecahedron]], a [[Kepler–Poinsot polyhedron]] with twelve [[pentagram]] faces.<ref>{{cite book |first=Magnus |last=Wenninger |authorlink=Magnus Wenninger |title=Polyhedron Models |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=1974 |isbn=0-521-09859-9|contribution=22: The great stellated dodecahedron|pages=40–42}}</ref>

Each edge of the triakis icosahedron has endpoints of total degree at least 13. By [[Kotzig's theorem]], this is the most possible for any polyhedron. The same total degree is obtained from the Kleetope of any polyhedron with minimum degree five, but the triakis icosahedron is the simplest example of this construction.<ref>{{cite journal
 | last = Zaks | first = Joseph
 | doi = 10.1007/BF02804013 | doi-access=free
 | issue = 4
 | journal = [[Israel Journal of Mathematics]]
 | mr = 720304
 | pages = 281–296
 | title = Extending Kotzig's theorem
 | volume = 45
 | year = 1983| hdl = 10338.dmlcz/127504
 | hdl-access = free
 }}</ref> Although this Kleetope has isosceles triangle faces, iterating the Kleetope construction on it produces convex polyhedra with triangular faces that cannot all be isosceles.<ref>{{cite journal
 | last = Eppstein | first = David | author-link = David Eppstein
 | doi = 10.1007/s00373-021-02314-9
 | issue = 4
 | journal = [[Graphs and Combinatorics]]
 | pages = 1247–1269
 | title = On polyhedral realization with isosceles triangles
 | volume = 37
 | year = 2021| arxiv = 2009.00116
 }}</ref>

==As a Catalan solid==
[[File:Triakis icosahedron.stl|thumb|3d model of a triakis icosahedron]]

The triakis icosahedron is a [[Catalan solid]], the [[dual polyhedron]] of the [[truncated dodecahedron]]. The truncated dodecahedron is an [[Archimedean solid]], with faces that are [[regular decagon]]s and [[equilateral triangle]]s, and with all edges having unit length; its vertices lie on a common sphere, the [[circumsphere]] of the truncated decahedron.{{sfnp|Williams|1979|p=88}} The [[polar reciprocation]] of this solid through this sphere is a convex form of the triakis icosahedron, with all faces tangent to the same sphere, now an [[inscribed sphere]], with coordinates and dimensions that can be calculated as follows.

Let <math>\varphi</math> denote the [[golden ratio]]. The short edges of this form of the triakis icosahedron have length <math>(5\varphi+15)/11 \approx 2.099 </math>, and the long edges have length {{nowrap|1=<math> \varphi+2 \approx 3.618</math>.<ref>{{Mathworld |urlname=TriakisIcosahedron |title=Triakis icosahedron }}</ref>}} Its faces are isosceles triangles with one obtuse angle and two acute angles of:<ref name=williams>{{cite book
 | last = Williams | first = Robert | authorlink = Robert Williams (geometer)
 | year = 1979
 | title = The Geometrical Foundation of Natural Structure: A Source Book of Design
 | publisher = Dover Publications, Inc.
 | page = 89
 | isbn = 978-0-486-23729-9
}}</ref>
<math display="block"> \begin{align}
 \cos^{-1} \frac{-3\varphi}{10} &\approx 119^{\circ}, \\
 \cos^{-1} \frac{\varphi+7}{10} &\approx 30.5^{\circ}.
\end{align}</math>

As a Catalan solid, its [[dihedral angle]]s are all equal
<math display="block"> \cos^{-1} \frac{6\varphi+3}{4\varphi+7} \approx 160.61^\circ.</math>

[[File:Triakis_icosahedron_hulls.svg|thumb|upright=1.35|Combining a dodecahedron and icosahedron to form the triakis icosahedron.{{clarify|reason=Is "hull" actually a convex hull or something?|date=March 2026}}]]
One possible set of 32 [[Cartesian_coordinate_system|Cartesian coordinates]] for the vertices of the triakis icosahedron centered at the origin (scaled differently than the one above) can be generated by combining the vertices of two appropriately scaled [[Platonic solid]]s, the [[regular icosahedron]] and a [[regular dodecahedron]]:<ref>{{cite journal
|title=Catalan Solids Derived From 3D-Root Systems and Quaternions
|first1=Mehmet
|last1=Koca
|first2=Nazife
|last2=Ozdes Koca
|first3=Ramazon
|last3=Koc
|year=2010
|journal=Journal of Mathematical Physics
|volume=51
|issue=4
|doi=10.1063/1.3356985 
|arxiv=0908.3272
}}</ref>
* Twelve vertices of a [[regular icosahedron]], scaled to have a unit circumradius, with the coordinates <math display=block>\frac{(0, \pm 1, \pm \varphi)}{\sqrt{\varphi^2 + 1}}       ,        \frac{(\pm 1, \pm \varphi, 0)}{\sqrt{\varphi^2 + 1}}       ,        \frac{(\pm \varphi, 0, \pm 1)}{\sqrt{\varphi^2 + 1}}.</math>
* Twenty vertices of a [[regular dodecahedron]], scaled to have circumradius <math display=block>\frac{2+\varphi}{3+2\varphi}\sqrt {\frac{3}{2-1/\varphi}}=\frac{1}{11}\sqrt {75 + 6\sqrt{5}}\approx 0.8548,</math> with the coordinates <math display=block>(\pm 1, \pm 1,\pm 1)\frac{\sqrt {25 + 2\sqrt{5}}}{11}</math> and <math display=block>(0, \pm \varphi, \pm \frac{1}{\varphi})\frac{\sqrt {25 + 2\sqrt{5}}}{11}       ,         
(\pm \frac{1}{\varphi}, 0 , \pm \varphi)\frac{\sqrt {25 + 2\sqrt{5}}}{11}       ,         
(\pm \varphi, \pm \frac{1}{\varphi},0)\frac{\sqrt {25 + 2\sqrt{5}}}{11}.</math>

==Symmetry==
In any of its standard convex or non-convex forms, the triakis icosahedron has the same symmetries as a regular icosahedron.<ref name=shep/>
The three types of [[axis of symmetry|symmetry axes]] of the icosahedron, through two opposite vertices, edge midpoints, and face centroids, become respectively axes through opposite pairs of degree-ten vertices of the triakis icosahedron, through opposite midpoints of edges between degree-ten vertices, and through opposite pairs of degree-three vertices.
